segments.text: A lot of kids in junior high school and high school feel different. But to be told no, it's not your imagination, you are different? This moment is something a lot of kids in special ed get to at some point or another: a shocking moment of understanding that they are not the same as other kids and that everybody else knew that long ago. segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our program, stories of people who were told that they're different: some who were comfortable with that, some who did not understand it, some who understood it and did not like it. We bring you stories of the developmentally disabled. It is a very different kind of show for us with voices and stories that usually do not make it to the radio.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life , distributed by Public Radio International. I'm Ira Glass. Our show today in three acts. Act One, Get On The Mic. In which we hear the story of what happens when you hand microphones to developmentally disabled people of various sorts and then send them out with camera crews to interview anyone they want on the streets of America. One thing that turns out to be on the minds of the disabled, same thing that's on your mind and mine, TV.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Two, Black Hole Son. In that story we hear from a mother and her son who, at three, became mesmerized with black holes and Stephen Hawking, an obsession which gave way to bunnies and flowers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, Walkout. Veronica Chater tells the story of her own brother, Vincent, who one day quit his job at an assisted learning center, and then quit everything else, mystifying everybody in his life. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, Get On The Mic. Here's a typical moment from the film, How's Your News? The film is a documentary in which five developmentally disabled people travel across America in an RV interviewing people they meet along the way. When they get to Texas, one of the reporters, Sue Harrington, is at a cattle auction talking to an auctioneer, an older guy wearing a cowboy hat. There's all sorts of talk about prices and cows. And then Sue, apropos of absolutely nothing, comes out with this question.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, How's Your News? team has an uncanny knack for bringing the sentimental out of people they meet. Arthur Bradford, who led the How's Your News? team across the country, he first got to know them in 1993 at a camp for disabled adults called Camp Jabberwocky. He was a counselor there teaching a video class. And as part of the class, he would take the campers out to do man-on-the-street interviews.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They did that for a few summers, and then decided that it might be exciting and fun to try to do their interviews on a two-week, cross-country trip, which became this movie. Arthur says that, from the start, it's been interesting to see how people react to the disabled reporters.

segments.speaker: Arthur Bradford
segments.text: What I've noticed is that, when someone with a disability approaches someone on the street, this is without a camera or anything, that person sort of settles into OK, I need to, I guess basically, talk down to this person. It's sort of like they're talking to a child, I would say. But what I like about when you give them a microphone and a camera is that, suddenly, the people take them a little more seriously. And I would say they, maybe, give them a little more respect.

segments.text: One of the facts of life for many disabled adults is that they don't get around that much. Many live in group homes. Most of their contact is with other disabled people. segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Two: Black Hole Son. Because of a very rare genetic disease, Sam was born with holes in several vital organs, including his heart and his brain. For his first five years, if one wasn't making his life hell, the other was. He's seven now. And recently his mom and he sat down together to talk about how things used to be and how they got much, much better.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: OK. So let me start interviewing you.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Can you describe yourself? What kind of a person are you?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: I'm nice and kindful person.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: You're kindful?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yes, and playful.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: What do you do that's nice?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Hug you.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: When I was pregnant with Sam, the first ultrasound came back that there was something wrong. I was thinking just please, let it be something with his body not with his brain. I can handle his body, but I'll be a bad mom to a retarded child. Everybody has their thing they can't take, and that's it for me.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: So when Sam was born, when he was five days old, he had heart failure. So then we learned about the deletion in the chromosome, velo-cardio-facial syndrome. So we didn't know if he was going to make it. And we had a talk with the geneticist. And he said if you give him the operations, it's not sure he'll pull through. But if he does, he's going to be retarded, probably. And I said OK. I don't care anymore. I want him, and I need him.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: What were you like when you were three years old?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: I was walking, but I was crying too.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Do you want to talk about what you used to be like?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: No way.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: He started torturing animals when he was three, and talking all the time about wanting to die. And he stabbed his stepfather with a plastic knife and drew blood, and poured boiling water on me, wiped things on the bus that should not be wiped.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: He was kicked out of school when he was four because they said he was a danger to himself and others. And so we took him to a psych unit, and he was studied for a few days. And that's when they told us about the bipolar, rapid-cycling bipolar, which is common in velo-cardio-facial syndrome. It has early-onset, and it hits you hard a lot of the time. And sometimes it doesn't, but it did in him. But nobody told me that.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: I want to show you a drawing that you did.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: That's me with heart faces and heart eyes.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: There's about 100 hearts in your face in this drawing.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Green hearts, how come? What were you feeling when you drew this?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: I was feeling like hugging you and kissing you and giving you cards.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: All your drawings now have a lot of hearts and flowers and birds, and people are smiling. Do you remember, when you were about four years old, do you remember what you drew all the time?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Black holes?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Do you know what you were feeling when you were drawing black holes every day?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Like, the black hole was going to suck the whole world up and make everybody die and end of the world.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Yeah. Did you feel like that a lot, like everybody was going to die?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: I think the first time Sam heard of a black hole, he was almost four. And we were watching Stephen Hawking, a show. At that time, he couldn't sit down for anything. He couldn't sit down for a 15-minute cartoon. But he was really into space. And this was the only time he sat down and he watched the boring show from start to finish. They had, I think it was like a '50s cartoon of a black hole on just for a second, you know, one of those swirly things. That just captivated him. He started drawing it all the time. In every family portrait, it'd be us and the black hole.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: At school, they had this rainbow bear notebook and it would have all the kids' drawings in there. And there would be, like, 19 drawings of kids going sledding, kids going to McDonald's, kids playing with their siblings or something. And then, on Sam's page, it would be a black hole destroying the universe or a black hole coming down the railroad tracks sucking up humans. I was kind of proud of his differentness and his imagination, but, at the same time, I knew that it was like this horror to him.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: What are some nightmares you've had?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: The moon, blowing moon.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: The moon blows on you?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: How come?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: I think of bad thoughts that time. I mean, bad thoughts.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: You had bad thoughts and that's why the moon blew on you?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Did the moon know you had bad thoughts?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: What would happen when the moon blew on you?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: I was scared and frightening.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: And you had that nightmare a lot, I think.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Two times.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: No. Like a whole year you had that nightmare.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Before he discovered black holes, it was any swirling thing that sucks you in. Like, even when he was months old, if he saw a ceiling fan, it was the only time he would quiet. He would just stare at that ceiling fan. I know a lot of babies do, but he just was obsessed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then, when he was three, he had an imaginary friend, but it wasn't a boy, it was a fan. But this one was called bad, bad fan. And its blades were teeth. And then it had these little, tiny eyes and these little, tiny feet at the bottom, and it would kill people. It would just blow on people and that would kill them because his breath was filled with teeth. And then, sometimes when he broke things, he said bad, bad fan did it. And it was kind of creepy, you know? It was just me and him living in the house. And you start thinking-- oh.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He had to destroy all day long. He had to. He couldn't not. He destroyed his favorite toys. He destroyed my favorite furniture, anything that meant anything, especially.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I used to watch The Sally Jessy Raphael Shows, or whoever it was that had all those shows about the out-of-control-- I think it was Montel-- had all the shows about the out-of-control, really young children. And the parents had to lock the door against them at night. And they lived in fear. And, supposedly, nobody could help.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I would always think well, you must be really bad parents. I would never have a problem with controlling my kid. I would teach them how to act. And if I had your kid for a week, he'd shape up. And so, of course, once I became afraid of my child, I didn't tell anyone because I thought they would think the same thing about me. And I kind of thought the same thing about me. You know, he'd be nice and normal, and then just do something so horrible and senseless.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it seemed like that to Sam too. He could never understand. He'd do something like try to break the cat's leg, something like that. And then, immediately afterwards, he'd be crying and saying, "I don't know why I did that." And he would be just as angry and sad as I was. And he'd say, "I don't understand." And he'd start punching himself and biting himself and putting bruises all over his body. Ugh! Oh, that was a horrible life.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Do you know why you take the pills every day?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Because my brain is all, like that.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: What is that? Nobody can see on the recorder. Describe it.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: It's so wild. And has to-- it's pumping blood all wild.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Pumping blood all wild?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: He started on a drug called Zyprexa. And within 24 hours we noticed a change. And then, after about 56 hours, it was like night and day. This was not the same kid at all. It's hard to believe that we were all living like we were. I mean, I can't believe it. When I sit here and talk about it, I can't believe that that existed and I didn't try to get a diagnosis earlier. I just kept on thinking I could not be such a bad parent and it would get cured. Or, I don't know what I thought.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: But, within two days after starting on the Zyprexa, we would go out. We could go to do three errands in one day. He could wait in line. He was doing well in school. I mean, it didn't happen overnight because he still at some bad memories, but he started to get some nice memories to put on top of the bad ones. And he just got nicer and nicer, and happier and sweeter. He stopped having nightmares. At first, he would ask me when his brain was going to be messed up again, but now he feels like it's his brain, you know? He feels like he's in control of his own brain.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Do you have any girlfriends?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah, only one. Who is it? Rose.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Aw. Tell me about Rose.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: She's kind and cute.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: What does she look like?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: I forget.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: She looks kind of like her mom, maybe.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Would you like to be married?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah! I would like to be.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: What is marrying like?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: You have a bride. And you are giving them flowers and heart and Valentines stuff.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: When I was doing these interviews with him, I realized something about him that I hadn't seen before, which is all those hearts and bunnies and rainbows that he talks about all the time, it's not because he's silly. It's because he's been through more pain and powerlessness than most people ever will in their whole life. And I think he took all that information about life, about what it is, what it means for him to be alive, and he made an informed decision that he's going to be happy with the good parts of life and he's going to spread them around. And I think he knows something about hearts and bunnies and rainbows. He's not like Forrest Gump, you know? It's not like-- you know, he came out of something very hard, and he has a very strong will.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Let's make up a story about a bad boy.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: [UNINTELLIGIBLE] boy?

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: No. That'd scare people out.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: That would scare people listening?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Let's make up a story about a human boy. What would he do in the day?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: He would just have fits. And then he would [UNINTELLIGIBLE] his bowl, and then he would spill it, like that.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: Push his bowl of food away and spill it?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: What else?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Break the bowl. And his mom will say, "You have to clean it up. And, after that, you will have to go right up to your room."

segments.speaker: Sam's Mother
segments.text: What would the boy be thinking?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: That he wants to be a nice boy. Then when he came back downstairs, he hugged everyone in the world. The end.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: Wow. That bad boy turned out to be a good boy. Do you know anyone like that?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.text: No. It's fake.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The mother who put that story together asked that we not broadcast her and her son's name.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [MUSIC - "KEEP THE SUNNY SIDE" BY THE WHITES]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, Walkout. Sun Kim has taught severely autistic children for the past five years. She says autistic kids, in general, tend to not understand social cues, and that her students, because of the severity of their autism, can't tell her their basic needs or thoughts. And so she finds she spends a lot of her work day trying to figure out what it is that they're thinking. And often, she's stumped.

segments.speaker: Sun Kim
segments.text: Sometimes you'll just see them looking off in the distance and laughing. You think what are they laughing about? What's so funny? Or when we ask them to do certain things, like pass out the place mats or pass out the cups, what's going through their head process? Like, OK, I'm supposed to do this and I don't-- or are they hearing just, murmur, murmur, verbiage, and not really understanding? Or just listening to the tonalities of what we're saying? Believe me, I've wanted to be inside their head just to know what they're thinking or feeling so many times.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This question, of course, was part of our story in Act Two. And it's at the heart of this next story. It's at the center of what it means to deal with certain kinds of people with developmental disabilities.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Veronica Chater's younger brother, Vincent, can't do math, even the simplest addition. He doesn't speak well. He has a version of what used to be called mental retardation. But, when he was a baby and doctors tried to diagnose him, they couldn't find anyone else with his particular combination of symptoms, and so they named his own syndrome after him: the Vincent syndrome.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He's an adult now. And for a while seemed to be doing just fine, until a point a few years ago when he surprised everybody in the family by quitting his job, and then quitting everything else in his life. And it was not clear to them why he did it and what it meant and what it would mean for his future. Veronica Chater put together this story.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Ever since Vincent quit his job, he spent more and more time alone in his room. At Christmas, at our parent's house in northern California, my brothers and sisters and I weave in and out of the kitchen, talking about work, telling jokes, and taking orders from Mom.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: There are 11 of us. I'm the second oldest. Vinnie's the fifth. As usual, he's nowhere to be seen. When I go down the hall, I find him in his bedroom with the door closed, drinking an orange soda from the can and watching an old movie.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: [SOUND OF TELEVISION]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: His face is close to the TV screen, about 10 inches away. And he has a serious expression, the kind you catch on a detective who's trying to crack a case. He could be 18 and he could be 50, you can't quite tell. He has a short little boy haircut. And, every day, he wears a sweatshirt with the words carpe diem on it. The truth is, he's 34.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Did Santa come and fill your stocking?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Indeed.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: What did you get in your stocking?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: [UNINTELLIGIBLE]. Jamaroonie.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Some jamaroonies?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Vinnie still lives in his childhood bedroom, which he calls his apartment. Ever since he retired, bit by bit, he's been withdrawing into his own little world, a world that doesn't include me or anyone else.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: OK, here we go. Cleaning up.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: My mom and dad still take care of Vinnie, but it's mainly my mom's job.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Clean it, clean you.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: Well, we'll shave you, shave you.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: My parents, who are devout Roman Catholics, were undaunted by the idea of having a, so-called, special needs child. They figured it was part of God's plan. He was an angel in our midst, as my dad always said. They refused to think of him as a burden, even though he would depend on them for the rest of their lives. Every morning, my mom readies him for the day: combing and gelling his hair, brushing his teeth, and shaving him.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: [SINGING] I like my clean-shaven man.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: She tilts his chin this way and that, handling him like a barber with an overbooked schedule.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: Done. All spiffed up for the day. OK, here.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Here we go.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: Put your shaver away, OK?

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: There are all sorts of little games that Vinnie and my mom play together all day long. Most of them are impenetrable to outsiders. He'll say, "Repeat. Repeat." And she'll reply, "Redeep in the redeep." And they'll both giggle.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: OK, so I'm going to test you. I want to see if you know any movies because you're always the one that knows movies. OK. Who said this? Who's the one that sucked his thumb and said, "Mommy"?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: The cartoon Robin Hood.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: Right. You got that one. I didn't know if you were going to get that.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Despite his disability, Vinnie has a really good memory for all sorts of trivia. Quizzing him about movies is the impromptu game my mom and dad play with him throughout the day, from morning till night.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Dad
segments.text: OK, I've got one for you, Vincent. See if you can get this one. [SINGING] It was a Monday. Ain't gonna soldier no more.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: The bond between them is more than a bond, it's a union for life. As Vinnie passed through his teenage years and became an adult, Mom saw to it that he was kept busy. She signed him up for bowling, for Special Olympics, and for pretty much every seasonal sport from basketball to badminton.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: But as he got older, Vinnie's personality grew darker and more mysterious. I didn't notice it right away. I don't think any of us did. Mom was so good at keeping Vinnie distracted from himself that it didn't seem like a problem. But two years ago, it grew too large to ignore.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Let's play games.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: I'm not playing games right now. Go get my sour cream. Come on. I want the sour cream. I can't make those chantilly potatoes without it.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Every time I go home, it hits me a little bit more that, even though Vincent and I are about the same age, my mom talks to him like he's a precocious four-year-old. And, more and more, I've noticed that he's aware of it too. When he returned without the sour cream and noticed that Mom and I were talking about him, he got upset.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: It is a wonderful reaction to talk about somebody? When you talk about me, I wonder.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: I talked right in front of you. I wasn't telling any secrets. I'm going to say what I'm going to say because it's true. There's nothing wrong with having the truth, is there?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: I'll put this away here--

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: You know, where it goes. Top shelf. The little slot, slide it in there. Thank you, very much.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: He can go from one minute to-- oh, yeah. Dad's so afraid he's going to get him angry, he won't give him any orders. I have to give all the orders. Yeah. If he wants to get smart with me, and I say, "God said you have to obey your parents I'm your mother. You do what I say, when I say. Da, da, da, da, da. Da, da, da, da." And he'll do something, sometimes I say, "You go in and you tell God you're sorry for that." He'll go in his room. And he comes out, "Sorry for talking like that." And I said, "That's fine, Vin. OK. We just don't do that." Then he gets in a really good mood after that.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: It might seem like my mom is rough on Vinnie, but I have to say that her way of dealing with him has pretty much worked out for the best, until the day Vinnie decided to retire. When he quit his job, Vinnie dropped everything including bowling, basketball, and the Special Olympics. Where once he was busy from dawn till dusk, now he had nothing to do, so he began sleeping to pass the time, up to 18 hours a day. It worried all of us, especially Mom. He was sleeping his life away, and we didn't understand why. It felt like we were losing him, like he was giving up, so I set out to figure out why.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: If you ask Vinnie about why he quit his job, you don't get much of an answer. In general, it's hard to get a direct response out of him on any subject. "Could be," he'll say, or, "Maybe." It's not clear he even knows what his own feelings are sometimes. Often, when any of us asks him about his job, he'll just change the subject, like he did when I asked him about it, sitting in Mom's kitchen.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: How come you don't just tell me why you quit?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: But seriously, it might be empty, blank there, after you were saying something.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: You mean you're leaving that section blank because you don't want to fill it in with words?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Blank is there before I finish words.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Are you playing word games with me now?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: We've all asked Vinnie dozens of times in dozens of different ways why he quit his job and everything else. And every time his answer is just as cryptic, and so we're all forced to guess what the real reasons are. My mom's best guess is that Vinnie put himself into early retirement and started all these dark moods because of a chemical change in his brain.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: The psychologist said he thinks there was a chemical imbalance that took place, suddenly, in his brain. And he prescribed Prozac for him.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Well, it's all chemical.

segments.speaker: Vincent's Mom
segments.text: I don't know. It's really a mystery to me what happened there.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Vinnie had worked for 12 years at a place called Concord Support Services, a company that hires mentally retarded adults and vocationally trains them. Vinnie always told me that he liked his job. He'd sit in a big warehouse with about 70 other disabled adults doing light assembly or stuffing envelopes. He made up to $60 a month, which, to him, was an infinite amount of money. We all assumed he'd found his place in the world.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Then, gradually, he started to become impatient and angry at work, threatening to break people's fingers if they touched him. He started disappearing into the work bathroom for up to an hour at a time just to get away from people. It was pretty clear that he was in a crisis.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: On his last day, he was wandering around looking for a bead he'd dropped. His supervisor asked him what he was doing. One thing led to another. Vinnie lost his temper. My parents were called in for a meeting. And Vinnie quit, just up and walked out.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: A few months ago, I asked Vinnie if he'd like to go back to his old job for a visit hoping it might spark something. I wasn't sure how he'd react, but he didn't even hesitate. He told me that he'd love to go. So the next morning, after my mom spiffed him up, we drove the route he'd taken for 12 years. When we arrived at the front doors, he's all smiles. He seems genuinely glad to be there.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I remember you.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: You do? Nice to see you.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: But, as we approach the warehouse floor where Vinnie used to work, his pace slows. At the warehouse door, he hesitates and purses his lips together.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: How are you?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Wonderful. Hi. Nice to see you [? Jane. ?]

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Nice seeing you.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: He becomes shy and looks confused as one person after another comes up to him. Some touch him fondly, one man blows in his face, and everyone stares. Vinnie tries to appear cool, but I can tell he's tense.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: We miss you, Vinnie. We miss the Vinnie Arnold we knew. We missed you, Vinnie. We missed you.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Would you like to begin basketball practice Saturday?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I don't know. I'm not into-- I'm back into bowling and running again.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: We hang out. And Vinnie looks uncomfortable, except when he decides, on his own, to busy himself cleaning and straightening. After 15 minutes, he disappears into the bathroom, his old hiding place. After a while, he comes out for a few minutes, then goes back in, and then comes back out again. When he heads back into the bathroom for the third time, I know it's time to leave.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Later, I talked to my brother, Danny, about it. Of all my siblings, Danny spends the most time with Vinnie. They go to movies, take walks, go to bookstores. Danny thinks Vinnie might have quit his job for all the normal reasons any of us quit a job. Maybe it had nothing to do with his disability.

segments.speaker: Danny
segments.text: I think he was probably extremely bored working in this place, doing the same thing over and over again: stuffing envelopes, putting paper clips in bags. There was no challenge to it, and I think it really frustrated him.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Vinnie might have simply had enough, enough of other people controlling his life. All the adults in his life were doing the sensible things you do for disabled people: giving structure to his days, coaxing his moods, all with the best intentions. It's possible that, in the end, that wasn't enough of a life. And so, one day, he changed the one thing in his life that he could. He said no to the one thing he could say no to and quit his job, and then quit everything else.

segments.speaker: Danny
segments.text: Being told what to do constantly, day in, and day out. And then he watches his other brothers and sisters running around and traveling and having their freedom, and here he is, stuck at home in his room. I can just imagine how frustrating that would be. It would make me angry if I was in that situation.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: After Vinnie retired, my mom and dad were determined to get him back into some kind of routine. After meeting with all sorts of social workers and suggesting dozens of ideas to Vinnie, they finally came up with something that he agreed to. They hired my brother, Bernard, to build a chicken coop in the backyard and to put Vinnie in charge of a miniature chicken farm. My mom had always wanted a chicken farm anyway. This was her big chance to get one.

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Vinnie took to every aspect of chicken farming. He was painstakingly mindful of the chicken's daily schedule of free-range feeding and lock-up. And he was especially fastidious about coop hygiene. But more than that, to everyone's surprise, he started participating in activities again. He started basketball practice. And he's training again for the Special Olympics.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Molly, Polly, Jeanette, and Lonnie, here.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: [CHICKEN CACKLE]

segments.speaker: Veronica Chater
segments.text: Pretty much at any time of the day, you can see Vinnie standing as still as a marble sculpture in the backyard beside the coop, his eyes half closed, and his palms cupping the breeze, thinking, or just listening to the sound of his hens. He named them after old friends and talks to them like children.
